verdict.headline: Two things changed this run.
verdict.detail: Two things changed this run. First, the standing lineup problem is fixed: Ryerson is placed and the fielded side is a full eleven again, so the cheapest and largest action on the board for the last several runs is finally done and closed. Second, and this is the one that matters beyond this matchday, the flip programme is being stood down. It is not losing money, but it has been spending recommendations for weeks on a trade that cannot pay, and the ledger now says so clearly enough that continuing would be wilful. The points plan is unchanged in target and changed in price: buy Neuhaus, sell Adamu to fund it, sell Tanaka once Neuhaus has actually landed. Nothing here is urgent in hours, but the Neuhaus listing expires tomorrow morning and the whole sequence wants to be finished well before the Friday lock.

sell.reason: Adamu goes first and the recommendation is unconditional, because it is the one move this run with no downside at all. He is not in the fielded eleven, so selling him cannot weaken the side; the squad stays at a legal fillable formation, so there is no under-eleven penalty; and he is the only player on the books whose value is currently falling, which means holding him costs a little more every tick. He is perfectly fit and this is not an injury sale, it is a surplus-and-depreciating sale, and it stands on its own even if the Neuhaus bid is never placed. Tanaka is the second sale and the ordering is the entire point: he is in the fielded eleven, so selling him before Neuhaus is actually in the squad would leave the side a body short and trigger the under-eleven penalty. Sell him at the moment Neuhaus lands, not before, and if the bid loses do not sell him at all.

Paying a real premium is justified here in a way it never is on a flip, because this is a body held for the rest of the season rather than a position unwound in a day. Sheraldo Becker was the better buy on paper and was rejected on arithmetic, not merit: he is the bigger upgrade and would allow a formation switch, but everything sellable without gutting the eleven still falls short of his ask, and the only way to close the gap drops the squad below eleven. movers.reason: The flip programme is being stood down, and this reverses the standing posture rather than pausing it. The edge itself is real and is not decaying: the daily tick on rising players re-measures at least as strong in the recent window as when it was first found, and the great majority of such players do rise. The problem is that the edge cannot be reached. Across nearly two hundred flip recommendations, almost all were lost, and the typical loss was not narrow: the winning bid usually cleared far above market value, by a multiple of the drift being harvested. That exhausts every bid level. Bidding market value exactly almost never wins, so it earns nothing while costing nothing. Bidding up by the size of the edge gives away the entire profit and still loses most of the time. Bidding what it would actually take to win about half the time means paying several times more than the asset is about to rise, which is a reliable loss. There is no price at which this trade works in this league. The important lesson is about the tripwire: previous runs were told to watch for the drift decaying as rivals crowded in, and the drift never decayed. The crowding showed up instead as a collapsed win rate while the measurement stayed healthy, which is why it went unnoticed for so long. Watch the hit rate, not the drift. The two listings that qualified on the old rules have been closed unexecuted rather than carried forward. What would genuinely revive this is a manager asking below market value, which is a different and real mechanism, and there are none on the board at the moment. The separate open question of whether Kickbase caps squad size is still unanswered, though it now matters much less, since throughput is not the binding constraint when the win rate is this low.
